processing: Flowers, buds or petals of the damask rose are dried and infused in hot water. No oxidation or roast is involved.
harvest_season: Picked when the roses are in bud or bloom; dates vary with the place and little is documented specifically for tea.
appearance_dry: Small, whole pink buds or loose dried petals.
appearance_wet: Buds keep their shape and open only slightly.
taste_profile: Strongly rose-scented with a gentle floral taste, a slight sweetness and a little astringency.

brewing.notes: Use one or two teaspoons of buds per cup and steep for about six minutes.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. It is a dried flower product, usually sold loose by origin, and is best when recent, since scent fades with age. Seller claims about high-altitude Kashan buds are common and hard to check.
description:
Damask rose tea is an infusion of the dried buds or petals of Rosa × damascena, drunk in the Middle East. Sellers usually tie the Iranian product to the Kashan area, including Ghamsar.

Processing is simply drying. Whole buds hold their form in the cup. Damask rose is often described as having a stronger, truer rose scent than Rosa centifolia.

The cup is light golden and more about aroma than body. Iranian medicinal-plant literature describes the flower as very fragrant with a sweet and astringent taste, and that is a fair guide to what to expect.

Buy for smell. Open the bag and look for a clear rose scent and intact colour, and be careful with health claims, which outrun the evidence.
history:
Damask rose has its place in Iranian medicinal-plant literature, which uses its flowers and petals. The tea as a distinct product is much less documented, and no clear origin or date is recorded for it.

Today it is sold in the West as a Persian or Iranian rosebud infusion, mostly through specialist tea and herb sellers.
